qs.q: Which breast stromal tumor is uniquely noted for being equally common in both males and females?
qs.e: Myofibroblastoma is made of myofibroblasts and stands out as the only breast tumor that is equally common in males and females. Other stromal lesions like fibroadenomas and phyllodes tumors overwhelmingly present in females.
qs.s: Stromal Tumors: Fibroadenoma & Phyllodes Tumor Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: An investigator is studying various benign and malignant breast masses. Which interlobular stromal tumor is known to be locally aggressive, invade adjacent tissues, but never metastasize?
qs.e: Fibromatosis is locally aggressive and invades surrounding structures like muscle, but it never metastasizes. In contrast, high-grade phyllodes tumors and angiosarcomas are capable of distant metastasis.
qs.s: Stromal Tumors: Fibroadenoma & Phyllodes Tumor Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A medical student is asked to differentiate between intralobular and interlobular stromal tumors of the breast. Which of the following is strictly an interlobular stromal tumor containing no epithelial component?
qs.e: Lipomas are purely interlobular stromal tumors composed of fat cells with no epithelial component. Fibroadenomas and phyllodes tumors arise from intralobular stroma and are biphasic tumors featuring both epithelial and stromal elements.
qs.s: Stromal Tumors: Fibroadenoma & Phyllodes Tumor Pathology: MCQs

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Stromal tumors are growths arising from connective tissue of organs, often benign but can be malignant. Diagnosis relies on histology, immunostains, and imaging. Management balances surgery, medical therapy, and surveillance.

sections.p: Stromal tumors originate from the supportive tissue of an organ, such as the stroma of the ovary, breast, or uterus. They are classified by cell type, benign or malignant behavior, and hormone activity.
b: Malignant: stromal sarcoma, granulosa cell tumor

t.b: Determines cell lineage and hormone receptor status; e.g., inhibin, calretinin for sex‑cord tumors, CD34 for fibrous tumors. Positive staining supports diagnosis.
Assesses size, vascularity, and invasion. A well‑circumscribed, hypoechoic mass suggests benign; irregular margins raise suspicion for malignancy.
Elevated estradiol or testosterone can indicate functional sex‑cord tumors. Normal levels do not exclude malignancy.
Provides tissue for histology and IHC when imaging is inconclusive. If unavailable, excisional biopsy may be needed.

sections.p: Malignant stromal tumors are staged by the FIGO system (ovarian) or TNM (other sites), incorporating tumor size, nodal involvement, and metastasis.

t.b: Detects distant metastases; a negative scan supports early stage.
Evaluates local invasion; high signal on T2 suggests sarcoma.

sections.p: Genetic mutations (MED12, FOXL2), hormonal imbalances, and chronic inflammation are common drivers. In low‑resource settings, infections like schistosomiasis or HIV may influence immune surveillance.
b: MED12 mutation in fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor

t.b: Immunosuppression may increase risk of aggressive stromal tumors.
Chronic pelvic inflammation can predispose to sarcomas.

sections.p: Symptoms vary by location: breast stromal tumors present as painless masses; ovarian stromal tumors may cause abdominal pain, menstrual irregularities, or virilization.
b: Pain or bleeding if large or invasive

sections.p: A stepwise approach combines imaging, serum markers, and tissue diagnosis.
Rapid growth, ulceration, or hormonal excess signals possible malignancy. Complications include hemorrhage, metastasis, and endocrine crises.
b: Signs of virilization or estrogen excess

sections.p: Treatment depends on benign vs malignant, size, and hormone activity. Surgery is mainstay; adjuvant therapy tailored to tumor type.
b: Avoid high‑dose steroids in low‑resource settings due to infection risk

sections.p: Regular imaging and hormone monitoring detect recurrence early. Prevention focuses on early detection and managing risk factors like chronic inflammation.
Benign stromal tumors can mimic epithelial breast cancers or other gynecologic masses.
Normal hormone levels do not exclude functional tumors; imaging may miss microscopic invasion.
b: Ultrasound may underestimate size of phyllodes tumor

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of virilization or estrogenic symptoms

faq.q: What is the most common benign stromal tumor of the breast?
faq.a: Fibroadenoma, often seen in young women.

faq.q: Can a stromal tumor be malignant?
faq.a: Yes, examples include stromal sarcoma and malignant granulosa cell tumor.

faq.q: Do stromal tumors always produce hormones?
faq.a: Only a subset, such as sex‑cord tumors, secrete hormones; most are non‑functional.
